Question: I want to treat rice seeds with Azospirillum and Phosphobacteria, how much water should I mix with 5 packets of each for soaking overnight?
AgentAnswer: If you are using five packets of Azospirillum and five packets of Phosphobacteria for your rice seeds, the instructions from the Indian extension guidelines say to add enough water so that the seeds are completely covered and let them soak overnight before you plant them. The guidelines do not give a specific number of litres or a ratio of water to seed, so just make sure the seeds are fully submerged in water for the whole night. That is the recommended way to treat the seeds with these inoculants. If you need a precise amount, you might want to ask your local agriculture office for more detail.

Question: After sowing rice seeds, how many days should I keep the seedbed completely flooded with water to avoid any problem?
AgentAnswer: Hey, after you sow rice, the official Indian guides do not give a set number of days to keep the seedbed fully flooded. They say keep the water on during the early growth stage and generally keep the field flooded for most of the season, but they don’t give a specific day count for the post‑sowing period. So there isn’t a fixed number to follow – just keep the water there as long as the early growth needs it, following the usual practice of staying flooded for the crop’s early days, and then continue flooding throughout the season as per your local routine.

Question: my paddy field soil is very fluffy. What can I do to prevent my animals and workers from sinking during puddling?
AgentAnswer: If your paddy soil feels soft and people or animals sink when you try to puddle it, the first thing you can do is make the ground firm with a simple stone roller. Take a 400 kg stone roller or a big oil drum full of stones and roll it over the field eight times when the soil is at a friable moisture level – that is when the soil feels just right, about 13 %–18 % moisture. Do this once every two or three years, because the benefit lasts for a few crops. Before you start rolling, plough the field and mix in 2–3 t ha⁻¹ of compost or well‑decomposed animal dung; if your soil is very sodic, add gypsum at half the amount you would normally need. After the roller work, flood the field to a shallow depth of about 2.5 cm – that is the depth that keeps the soil at the right moisture for puddling without making it too soft. Then use a cage‑wheel or a cage‑wheel plus rotavator to puddle; two passes with the cage‑wheel give a good puddling effect. While you are doing this, build temporary walkways or small bunds around the puddling area so that animals and workers stay on firm ground. Once you finish puddling, let the soil sit for a few days before you transplant your rice. This simple plan, which costs about Rs 250 per hectare and can give a profit of roughly Rs 1 200 per hectare, is what Indian extension services recommend to keep your field firm and prevent sinking during puddling.

Question: I am from Tirunelveli, I planted early kar rice in April-May, but it is not growing well. Can I use ASD 16 or ASD 18 varieties for replanting in July-August for kar rice?
AgentAnswer: Sure, you can try re‑planting with the ASD 16 rice variety in July or August because it is a short‑duration type that matures in about 110‑115 days and is known to grow well in the Kar season in Tirunelveli if you give it enough water. The plan is to sow 20 kg of seed per hectare, either by broadcasting or laying lines, and treat the seed with 3 packets of Rhizobium and 3 packets of Phosphobacteria mixed with water 24 hours before you sow. Before you plant, spread 25 kg of urea, 120 kg of DAP and 40 kg of potash over the field, and keep the soil moist. After sowing, flood the field and give a “life” water on the third day, then water every 7 to 10 days, keeping 5‑10 cm of water during the growing stage and 2‑3 cm when the panicle starts to form. About two weeks after transplanting, if the leaves look pale, give another 40 kg of urea. Hand‑weed the field whenever weeds appear and only use chemicals if the weeds become severe. Watch out for blast, bacterial leaf blight and the brown‑plant‑hopper; if you see these problems, you can spray mancozeb at 1000 g per hectare or carbendazim at 250 g per hectare, but only when symptoms show up. ASD 18 is not recommended for re‑planting because there is no reliable information about its growth time, yield or water needs, so it is safer to stick with ASD 16 until more data become available. If you follow this simple package, you should be able to get a good second crop of rice in your area.

Question: my White Ponni paddy yield is only 5500 kg per hectare, how can I increase it to 6200 kg like the other farmers in my area?
AgentAnswer: Hey, to try and bring your White Ponni yield up to about 6200 kg per hectare, one thing that many farmers in your area use is a seed soak with a special bacteria mix before sowing. You can get a packet of Azospirillum and a packet of Phosphobacteria – each packet is about 600 g per hectare – or a single packet of a product called Azophos that gives you 1200 g per hectare. Mix the packet or the two packets with enough water to cover the seeds and soak them overnight before you put them in the nursery bed. If you have a bottle of Azospirillum biofertilizer, you can take 4-5 ml of that and mix it with 50-100 ml of water and spray it on the seeds before you spread them. The idea is to give the seeds a good soak so the bacteria can stick to them. The exact amount of water to use is not given in the research, but you just need enough water to fully cover the seeds and let them sit overnight. After you sow, the research does not say how long to keep the bed flooded, so you might follow what your neighbours do or ask the local agriculture office for that part. If you can get the same seed soak and use the right amount of the bacterial mix, it could help your yield get closer to the 6200 kg figure. I’m not 100% sure about every detail, so it would be good to check with the supplier for the exact mix and also talk to your local office for any other tips that fit your field.

Question: my paddy crop in Nagapattinam district is flooded during NE monsoon, how to manage waterlogged soil for better yield?
AgentAnswer: First, cut a shallow channel about 45 cm wide and 60 cm deep or use a small pump to lower the water to about 5 cm in the field; if the water stays, keep the pump or siphon until the depth is 5 cm, then when the field is drier roll the soil with a 400 kg stone roller about eight times while the soil is at 13‑18 % moisture and keep a 2.5 cm water layer on top while you roll so the soil becomes firm; add about half of the gypsum needed and spread 5 t of green leaf manure 10‑15 days before transplanting, or use 25 t of farmyard manure; if the field feels very soft, build raised beds 1‑2 m wide and 0.3‑0.5 m high using a mix of local soil, 2‑3 t of compost and 2‑3 t of well‑rotted farmyard manure, then puddle the beds with a 2.5 cm water layer; for nutrients give a total of 100 kg of nitrogen split 50 % at the start, 25 % after 30 days, and 25 % after 60 days; give 35‑50 kg of phosphorus and 35‑80 kg of potassium as a base, and spread 25 t of farmyard manure when you plough; if you need a quick boost mix 22 kg urea, 18 kg gypsum, 4 kg neem cake and 17 kg potash per acre and spray while a thin water film is on the leaves; spray a small amount of zinc solution (2 kg urea + 1 kg zinc sulfate

Question: For one hectare transplanted rice, how much nursery area and seed rate should I plan for a wet nursery?
AgentAnswer: For one hectare of rice that you will transplant, you need about 800 square metres of wet nursery area, which is the same as 20 cents of your farm. The amount of seed you sow in that nursery depends on the type of rice you grow: if it is a short‑duration variety use about 60 kilograms of dry seed, for a medium‑duration variety use 40 kilograms, for a long‑duration variety use 30 kilograms, and for a hybrid variety use 20 kilograms. These numbers are the standard recommendations from the Tamil Nadu Agricultural University and are used by many farmers in India for wet nurseries.

Question: My rice nursery seedlings will be pulled out after 25 days. When should I apply DAP in the nursery and in what dose?
AgentAnswer: If your seedlings will be pulled out after 25 days, you should give them the DAP fertilizer either when you prepare the nursery or about 10 days before you pull them out, which is around the 15th day of the nursery. The amount you need is 40 kilograms of DAP for every hectare of your nursery, which is the same as putting 2 kilograms of DAP in each 40‑square‑meter patch of your nursery. That is all you need to follow the guidelines for a 20‑25 day nursery.

Question: What is the suggested seed treatment schedule with fungicide and Pseudomonas fluorescens for rice before sowing in the nursery?
AgentAnswer: First clean the rice seed and let it dry. If you want to harden it, soak it in a 1 % KCl solution (one part seed to one part solution) for 16 h and then keep it in shade until it can be stored. Next, put the disease‑killer carbendazim on the seed at a rate of 2 g per kg of seed; mix it with about 5 ml of water for each kg of seed and let it sit for 1–2 h. After that, add the helpful bacteria Pseudomonas fluorescens at 10 g per kg of seed (or 5 ml of the liquid form per kg of seed) and stir well so it sticks to the seed. Then soak the treated seed overnight, 12–16 h, in water at the usual temperature (some people prefer 18 h). Drain the extra water, let the seed dry a little so it is not wet on the outside, and plant it right away in a wet nursery bed. If you wish, you can also mix a single dose of Azophos, Azospirillum or Phosphobacteria, each at 1 kg per hectare, with the seed slurry when you sow.

Question: I have treated my rice seed with Pseudomonas fluorescens and soaked it overnight. If I want to sow immediately, what should I do with the soaked seeds?
AgentAnswer: After you have soaked the rice seed overnight, first pour out the extra water so the seeds are only damp and not swimming. Then spread them on a clean surface in the shade and let them dry for about 15 minutes so the surface moisture is gone and they don’t stick together. If you want, you can add 1 kg per hectare of Azophos or 1 kg per hectare of Azospirillum and Phosphobacteria to the seed before you sow. When you plant, put the seed at a depth of 3 to 5 centimeters in the field. Use the normal seed rate of 75 kilograms per hectare of dry seed, or the rate that matches your rice variety. Sow the seeds evenly, either by broadcasting or line‑sowing, so they are not crowded. After sowing, water the seedbed lightly, flooding it with 5 to 10 centimeters of water to keep the soil moist for germination. This way the Pseudomonas treatment stays effective and the seeds stay healthy.

Question: There are no soil test results for my wheat field. What blanket NPK dose and split application schedule should I follow?
AgentAnswer: If you don’t have a soil test, use the blanket recommendation. For well‑drained loamy soil like in Punjab and Haryana give 120 kg of nitrogen, 60 kg of phosphorus and 40 kg of potassium per hectare. Spread the nitrogen as 60 kg at sowing, then 30 kg when the plants are 25–30 days old, and another 30 kg when they are 40–45 days old. Put all the phosphorus and potassium at sowing. If your land is heavy clay like in parts of UP, Bihar or Odisha give only 40 kg nitrogen, 20 kg phosphorus and no potassium; split the nitrogen the same way: 20 kg at sowing, 10 kg at 25–30 days, 10 kg at 40–45 days. If you do not know the soil type, use the average: 60 kg nitrogen, 30 kg phosphorus and 30 kg potassium per hectare, split nitrogen the same way and put all phosphorus and potassium at sowing.

Question: I am cultivating TKM 11 rice, which is listed as 110–120 days duration, but my crop is maturing in about 100 days. Could it still be TKM 11?
AgentAnswer: Yes, it can still be TKM 11. That variety was bred to finish in as few as 100 days under good conditions, and it can grow faster if the weather is warm, if you sow early, keep the field well‑watered and give the plants good nutrients. The 110‑120 day figure is just a general rule, not a hard limit. If you want to be sure, look at other features of the plant, like how tall it grows, what the grains look like and whether it has the same disease resistance, or ask for a seed label that says it is TKM 11.

Question: For transplanted rice, how does the recommended seed rate vary between small‑, medium‑ and bold‑seeded varieties?
AgentAnswer: I’m sorry, I don’t have a confirmed answer for how the seed rate changes for small, medium or bold seeded rice varieties. The official guidelines only give a general rate of 7–8 kg ha⁻¹ when you plant one seedling per hill and 12–15 kg ha⁻¹ when you plant two seedlings per hill. Those are the numbers I can share with you right now. If you need more detail, it would be best to ask your local agriculture office for the specific recommendation for your variety.

Question: Our family owns 1.5 hectares of cultivable land in the village and we actively farm it. Are we eligible for PM-KISAN benefits?
AgentAnswer: Yes, you can get the PM‑KISAN benefit. You own 1.5 hectares, which is less than the 2 hectare limit for the scheme, and you are a farmer, not a salaried worker. If your family income is below ₹8 lakh a year and you have a bank account that is linked to your Aadhaar, you can apply. You will get ₹6,000 each year for you, or ₹12,000 if the whole family works together. You can apply through the PM‑KISAN portal or by going to your nearest bank or village office. If you are already getting other central farm help, you might not be able to get this money. If you are unsure about your income or the bank link, it is best to check with the local agriculture office.

Question: My family owns 3.5 hectares of land in the records. We are farmers but our area is above 2 hectares. Can we register for PM-KISAN?
AgentAnswer: Sorry, PM‑KISAN is only for families with up to 2 ha of cultivated land. Since your holding is 3.5 ha, you do not qualify for this scheme.

Question: I am a small farmer but I filed income tax last year due to some non-farm income. Will this make me ineligible for PM-KISAN?
AgentAnswer: Yes, if you filed an income‑tax return last year because you earned money from a job or other non‑farm work, you will not be able to get the PM‑KISAN benefit. The rule says that any family that has paid income tax, no matter if it was from farming or not, is not allowed to receive the scheme’s help, as long as the land you own is 2 ha or less. This rule is still the same in Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh and has not changed recently. So, because you filed a tax return, you are not eligible for PM‑KISAN. If you want to know about other ways to get help, you can ask your local agriculture office for more options.

Question: My father receives a government pension of ₹12,000 per month from a higher post, and I farm our land. Can our family still get PM-KISAN?
AgentAnswer: I’m sorry to say that, because your father gets a pension of ₹12,000 a month, the family does not qualify for the PM‑KISAN benefit of ₹6,000 a year. The rule says that if any family member gets a government pension of ₹10,000 or more per month, the whole family is excluded. If you ever want to check or ask again, you would normally need to bring an Aadhaar card for e‑KYC, the land‑holding record (like the title or crop‑holding certificate), your bank account details for the Direct Benefit Transfer, and a pension slip that shows the amount. If the pension were below ₹10,000 and no one had paid income tax, then you could apply, but with the current amount it is not possible. If you have any doubts, it’s best to talk to the local agriculture office for more help.

Question: Our names were added to the PM-KISAN list but payments have not started. What verification steps must the state follow before funds are released?
AgentAnswer: First the state makes a list of all farmer families that own 2 hectares or less of land as of 1 February 2019 and puts it in a computer file that the central portal can read. Then it checks that each name has a valid Aadhaar number and that this Aadhaar is linked to the bank account that will receive the money. The bank account number, its code and that it is an active savings account linked to Aadhaar are also checked by the bank system. After that the state looks again at the official land records to make sure the land is in the farmer’s name and that the area does not exceed 2 hectares. Once the computer checks are clear, a district officer goes to the village and visits each farmer to see the land title book, verify the Aadhaar card, the name and address, the bank details, and to make sure the family does not fall into any excluded group such as high‑income or pensioners. After the first payment is made, the state must physically check 5 percent of the farmers – 2.5 percent chosen by the central office and 2.5 percent chosen by the state – and this check has to be finished within 45 days of getting the list. Only after all these steps are finished and the state’s top officer signs off the final list does the central Direct Benefit Transfer system send the ₹2,000 to the farmer’s bank account every four months. If any step is missing or wrong, the state will stop the payment until it is fixed.

Question: As a small farmer, how and when will I receive the three PM-KISAN installments during the year?
AgentAnswer: You will get a total of ₹6,000 in a year, split into three equal parts of ₹2,000 each. The money is sent straight to the bank account that is linked to your Aadhaar number. The first payment comes after the state checks and approves your name on the list. After that, the next two payments are made automatically after about four months each, as long as your bank details stay the same. So you can expect the money roughly in the first part of the year, around January, then again around May, and the last one around September. If your bank details change or there is a problem, the payment will not be made until you correct it. That is how the schedule works.

Question: I am a marginal farmer and want to use PM-KISAN money mainly to buy fertilizer. Is that allowed or are there restrictions on how I spend it?
AgentAnswer: Yes, you can use your PM‑KISAN cash for buying fertilizer. The scheme lets you spend the money on agricultural inputs such as fertilizers, seeds, pesticides, and other farm‑related items. Just keep the purchase receipts as proof that the money was used for farming purposes.

Question: I need working capital for crop cultivation, buying fertilizer and also some money for household expenses. Can a single Kisan Credit Card cover all these needs?
AgentAnswer: Yes, a single Kisan Credit Card can give you money for all those things. It is a revolving credit that lets you borrow for crop cultivation, buying fertilizer, household expenses and even keeping your farm equipment in good shape. The credit limit is split into parts: the main part for growing your crop, a small part equal to 10 % of that main part for your household needs, and another part equal to 20 % of the main part to keep your farm assets working. The total limit you can get is ₹5 lakh per farmer, and you can borrow up to ₹2 lakh without any collateral. So you can use the card to get the money you need for seeds, fertilizer, and also for your family’s everyday expenses, all under one card.

Question: We are marginal farmers with very small holdings. How does KCC fix the loan limit for us if we do not have much land as security?
AgentAnswer: When you want a KCC loan, the bank first looks at how much land you plan to grow on and what crop you will plant, not just the size of your land. They decide a basic credit amount that matches that crop area and the cost of seeds, water and other things you need. Then, the bank gives you a free part of that amount that does not need any security – up to ₹2 lakh for you. If the crop area needs more money, you can borrow up to a total of ₹5 lakh, but you have to give the bank a promise that the future harvest will be used to pay back the loan, or you can give a warehouse receipt or a guarantee from someone else. So even if you have no land to put up as a mortgage, you can still get up to ₹2 lakh without any security, and you can get more up to ₹5 lakh if you can promise to pay back with the crop or other accepted guarantees. This rule is the same for all states, so it does not matter if you are in Uttar Pradesh, Punjab or Tamil Nadu. The bank will check your land records if you have any, look at your crop plan, add the free part, and then decide the rest with crop hypothecation or other securities. That is how the KCC decides the loan limit for marginal farmers like you.

Question: If I take a Kisan Credit Card, will I get an ATM-like card and can I withdraw money multiple times during the season?
AgentAnswer: Yes, a Kisan Credit Card comes as a normal ATM‑like debit card that you can use at any bank or micro‑ATM. You can take cash out more than once during the growing season, but there are limits: one withdrawal cannot be more than 10 % of the total credit limit, you can only take out up to 25 % of the limit in one day, 50 % in a month, and the total you can get in the whole season is the whole limit. The card can also be used for buying seeds, fertilizers, irrigation, post‑harvest work and even household needs, all within that same credit limit.

Question: I am worried about crop loss from heavy rain and hailstorm. What stages and risks does Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana cover for my crop?
AgentAnswer: If you are worried about heavy rain or hail hurting your crop, the PMFBY scheme can help you. It protects your crop from the moment you plan to sow it, through the time you plant, while the crop grows, and even up to 10 days after you harvest. It covers many natural problems, such as heavy rain, hail, floods, drought, storms, and pest attacks. If you have a valid policy for a crop that is listed in the scheme and you are 18 or older, you can claim. To get the money, you need to show proof of the damage, a weather report that says it rained a lot or it hails, and a certificate that tells how much you harvested. You can file the claim online or ask your insurance agent to do it, and you have to do it within about a month of the loss. The agent will check your documents, then the insurance will pay you the compensation. That is how the scheme works for heavy rain and hail.

Question: My Soil Health Card shows low phosphorus and potassium but normal nitrogen. How should I change my fertilizer use based on this card?
AgentAnswer: Your Soil Health Card shows you have enough nitrogen but not enough phosphorus and potassium. So you should keep the nitrogen at the same level that the card says, and add the full amount of phosphorus and potassium that the card recommends. Use DAP or SSP for phosphorus and KCl or MOP for potassium. Mix them into the soil before you sow or transplant. Add about 7.5 kg/ha of enriched farm‑yard manure at the same time. If your soil is acidic (pH below 6.5) you can add about 25 kg K₂O + 40 kg sulphur of gypsum or raise the pH with lime. If the card shows any micronutrient deficiencies, add zinc, boron, iron, manganese or sulphur together with the basal mix. You can also dip the seeds in a small amount of Azospirillum or another bio‑fertiliser. After the crop starts growing, split the nitrogen into three parts: give about one‑third of the total nitrogen 30 days after sowing, another one‑third 45 days after, and the last one‑third 60 days after, or according to the crop’s growth stages. Follow the exact numbers printed on your Soil Health Card for each nutrient; the card tells you how much, while the advice above tells you what to do and when.

Question: How often will soil samples be tested and Soil Health Cards updated for my fields under the national scheme?
AgentAnswer: Under the national Soil Health Card scheme, your soil is usually tested once every three years, and a new Soil Health Card is issued after each test. Some states may do it more often, but the standard interval is every 3 years.

Question: My rice nursery soil is very poor and I will pull out seedlings in about 22 days. How much DAP should I apply now, and is there an alternative if DAP is not available?
AgentAnswer: In a very poor soil rice nursery you should spread 40 kg of DAP on every hectare, which is the same as 2 kg of DAP for every one percent of the nursery area, and do this before the last puddling, about ten days before you pull out the seedlings. If you cannot find DAP, you can use other P‑fertilisers: give about 115 kg of single super‑phosphate or about 38 kg of mono‑ammonium phosphate on every hectare, and apply them the same way as DAP. It is a good idea to check with your local agriculture office or a nearby agronomist to confirm the exact amount if you have a soil test that says something different.

Question: I have soaked rice seeds overnight with Pseudomonas fluorescens as biocontrol treatment but suddenly need to sow them today. How can I make the seeds ready quickly for sowing?
AgentAnswer: I don’t have confirmed details about using Pseudomonas fluorescens for rice seed soaking. If the seeds were soaked overnight, you can simply sow them now as they are ready. If you want to be sure, rinse them in clean water to remove any excess liquid, then dry them a little on a clean cloth and plant them straight away. For the best guidance on this specific treatment, it would help to ask your local agriculture office or the supplier who gave you the bacteria.

Question: In my Kuruvai rice nursery, blast and brown spot are appearing. I have Pseudomonas fluorescens available. How should I use it for seed and nursery treatment?
AgentAnswer: In your Kuruvai rice nursery, you can use the Pseudomonas fluorescens you have by first treating the seeds before sowing: take 10 grams of the bacterial powder for every kilogram of dry seed, dissolve it in clean water – about 1 litre of water for each 100 grams of seed – and stir well to make a smooth mix. Put the seeds in this mix and let them soak for about 12 to 16 hours overnight at normal temperature. After soaking, pour off the extra water, spread the seeds out in a shaded area and let them dry for about 15 minutes until their moisture is back to about 8–9 percent; then sow them at a rate of 75 kilograms per hectare and plant each seed 3 to 5 centimetres deep. Do not add any carbendazim or other fungicides to the seed slurry because they can kill the bacteria; if you need a fungicide, apply it before the bacterial treatment and wait at least a day. Once the seedlings are out, treat the nursery soil by making a suspension that contains 10 to the eighth power of bacterial cells per millilitre – this is the standard count for the strain you have – and apply 500 millilitres of this suspension per hectare as a soil drench around the base of each seedling row, or you can mix about 2.5 kilograms of the formulation with 10 litres of water and spray it over the nursery bed. Give the first application when the seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves, which is about 7 to 10 days after transplanting, and give a second application 20 to 25 days after transplanting before the plants head. This two‑step application keeps a good population of the bacteria in the soil and on the roots, helping to fight blast and brown spot. If you notice any leaf damage after treatment, check that no incompatible chemicals were used. That is the recommended way to use Pseudomonas fluorescens in your rice nursery according to the verified research data.

Question: I skipped Pseudomonas seed treatment but want to protect my rice nursery now. Can I still use Pseudomonas fluorescens, and in what way?
AgentAnswer: Yes, you can still use the Pseudomonas fluorescens treatment even after you missed the earlier window. First, if you want to, soak the dry rice seed in a little saltwater that is 1 % KCl, 1 part seed to 1 part water, for 16 hours – this helps the seed stay strong and ready for the coating. Then take about 10 g of the Pseudomonas formulation for every 1 kg of seed and spread it evenly over the hardened seed, or if you did not soak it, do it on the dry seed. After coating, put the seeds in clean water, one part seed to one part water, and let them sit overnight, about 12 hours, so the bacteria can stick to the seed coat. When you are done, drain the extra water and lay the seeds on a clean tray, letting them dry in the shade for about 15 minutes until their moisture comes back to 8–9 %. Now you can sow the seeds at a rate of 75 kg per hectare and plant them 3 to 5 cm deep; you can do this the same day because the bacteria stay alive for at least 24 hours. If you prefer not to coat the seeds, you can make a liquid mix of the same formulation at about 10 g per litre and apply 500 ml per hectare as a soil drench or dip the roots at the time you transplant. Be careful not to use any fungicides such as carbendazim or thiram within 24 hours of giving the bacteria, because they can kill it, but you can still use insecticides or bio‑fertilizers like Azospirillum or Rhizobium as normal. No special safety gear is needed for the coating step, just handle the product as the label says. This way you will give your seedlings a protective layer against blast, brown spot and other leaf diseases, and it will also help them grow early.

Question: I want to replace part of my granular DAP in irrigated wheat with Nano DAP foliar spray. What is the recommended dose per acre per spray and how many sprays should I plan?
AgentAnswer: I’m sorry, but I don’t have any confirmed information about how much Nano DAP you should spray on wheat or how many times to spray it. The data I have only talks about seed soaking for rice and general water practices, not about wheat or foliar sprays. It would be best to ask your local agricultural office or the person who supplies the Nano DAP for the exact dose and spray schedule you need.

Question: I am currently using only urea for nitrogen in a cereal system. If I replace half of this nitrogen with composted manure, what changes in soil nitrogen and carbon can I expect over time?
AgentAnswer: I’m not sure about the exact changes in soil nitrogen and carbon if you replace half of your urea with composted manure, because the research data I have does not cover that. I suggest you talk to your local agriculture office or a nearby farmer extension officer who can give you reliable information for your specific field.
